title: Shooter in killing spree had privately made guns, coroner hears
article: When he was killed by police, Abdulla Shaikh had two privately constructed 9-millimetre semi-automatic handguns, 190 rounds of ammunition and a device that could have allowed him to fire 20 rounds per second, a firearms expert told a coroner's inquiry.

Shaikh also had images on his electronic devices indicating he had studied how to assemble such weapons from parts, said Montreal police Det.-Sgt. Marc-André Dubé, part of an RCMP team that conducts firearms investigations.
Police found photos of parts as well as information about the tools required.

"We can't conclude with certainty that he assembled the firearms himself, (but) we have fairly convincing evidence that he learned a lot about the field of private manufacturing, especially about these types of firearms," said Dubé, testifying on Tuesday afternoon.
Shaikh, 26, killed three people randomly within 24 hours in August 2022 before he was killed in an exchange of gunfire with police, the inquest has heard.
Police later determined Shaikh's gun had jammed after he fired at officers who burst through the door of his room at a motel in St-Laurent borough.
Coroner Géhane Kamel is conducting an inquiry into the deaths of Shaikh and his three victims.
Dubé told Kamel that since about 2016, Canadian police forces have seen a proliferation of firearms assembled from parts, often easily ordered online from the United States.

Unlike commercially manufactured firearms, these so-called ghost guns don't have serial numbers and are almost impossible to trace. They can be inexpensive to assemble and can be fitted with high-capacity magazines, Dubé said.
After Shaikh was killed, police found one weapon in his motel room and another in his nearby car.
Both were Glock-style handguns. The weapons seized are prohibited in Canada because the barrels are less than 105 mm in length, Dubé said.
The one found in the car was modified with a device, known as a Glock switch, that turns the semi-automatic weapon into an automatic one that can theoretically fire 1,200 rounds per minute, he added.
"Having fired one at a military installation, I can tell you they are ... very difficult to control," Dubé said of a handgun with a Glock switch.

Found in the motel room were seven high-capacity magazines, each of which could hold between 15 and 33 rounds, Dubé said. An eighth magazine was found in the car, this one able to hold up to 10 rounds.
He said police were not able to trace where Shaikh obtained the firearms and magazines or whether he had purchased parts to put the firearms together.

On Monday, Kamel heard that Shaikh killed André Lemieux, 64, and Mohamed Salah Belhaj, 48, on two Montreal streets on Aug. 2 before driving to Ontario and visiting the Toronto Zoo and Canada's Wonderland amusement park the next morning.
Shaikh then returned to Quebec and killed Alexis Lévis-Crevier, 22, on a residential street in Laval on the night of Aug. 3.
Police found no links between Shaikh and his victims, concluding he had chosen them at random.

Months before he was killed, an administrative tribunal decided Shaikh could continue residing outside a mental-health institution. He had been released from the institution in 2021, even though a psychiatrist determined he represented "a significant risk to public safety due to his mental state."
His family told police that Shaikh was diagnosed with schizophrenia and did not take his medication regularly.
On Wednesday at the inquiry, Lévis-Crevier's sister told Kamel she lives with a tremendous amount of grief over the loss of her younger brother.
Roxanne Lévis-Crevier said her brother lived just three blocks from her home in Laval, and was a frequent presence at her apartment and a popular uncle to her three children.
He was gunned down while skateboarding. Roxanne Lévis-Crevier learned of the incident on her street through Facebook while at a friend's house and texted her brother about it, but didn't hear back.
It was only in a middle-of-the night phone call from her father that she learned her brother was the victim.
She said the hardest thing about grieving her brother is that her children remember him well and are aware of what happened.
